items.question: How did you judge success in your early work using simulation and reinforcement learning to teach legged robots?
items.object: Success in early simulation-based reinforcement learning for legged robots
items.answer: So when I started, we were trying to use simulation with reinforcement learning to teach legged robots very simple things, like just walking on flat ground. And when the robot could take a few steps, that was already a big success. And the core focus was to reduce the training time needed to achieve that.
quotes: So when I started, we were trying to use simulation with reinforcement learning to teach legged robots very simple things, like just walking on flat ground. And when the robot could take a few steps, that was already a big success. And the core focus was to reduce the training time needed to achieve that.

The response identifies reducing the training time needed to achieve basic locomotion as the central focus of Nikita Rudin’s early work on legged robots.

items.question: What did you find compelling about demonstrating reinforcement learning live on the ANYmal quadruped?
items.object: Live demonstration of reinforcement learning on the ANYmal quadruped
items.answer: We were really trying to reduce the training time needed to achieve that. Before I started, there were some results of reinforcement learning for such quadrupeds, but it would take weeks of computation to achieve anything. Using GPUs and massively parallel simulators, we managed to reduce that to just a few minutes. We had a demo on stage at some point at a conference where we were running training live on a laptop while I was holding the robot. Every 15 seconds the laptop would send the latest policy to the robot, and you could literally see how it went from just falling over to taking a first step. After three or four minutes, it would be able to walk around the stage. That was a pretty cool visual demo for everyone to see exactly how the learning process happens.

items.question: What would it take for you to consider robot locomotion solved?
items.object: The standard for considering robot locomotion solved
items.answer: I had this debate so many times, even with my colleagues at NVIDIA and ETH. The general question is: is locomotion solved or not? We already had this debate five years ago, when the robot could just barely walk on flat ground and people were saying, “Yeah, locomotion is solved. We don't need to focus on it anymore.” My take was always, “No. Until the robot can really go anywhere a human can go, and you don't even need to think about whether it can do it or not, how reliable it is, then locomotion is not solved.”

The response states that solving robot locomotion requires reliability that people can take for granted.

items.question: How do you understand the difficulty of adding terrain perception to robot locomotion?
items.object: Blind versus perception-based robot locomotion
items.answer: Where we are today is that anything that is blind can be very robust. Blind meaning that the robot does not perceive its terrain, so it's just reacting. That makes the training much easier because you just have to throw a lot of things at it. It always tries to be stable. Especially for a quadruped, it's very easy to remain stable. For example, you can even walk upstairs. It will just hit the first step, realize there is something, and then climb up. With perception, you want it to actually react. You don't want it to hit the first step. You want it to place the feet much more carefully. That's harder. Today, at the end of 2025, we can have fairly good policies that plan the sequence of actions based on perceptive inputs. Because we're training everything in simulation, this means we need to be much more careful in how we simulate those sensors as well, and put a lot of effort into creating complicated terrain that can be seen by the cameras and all sorts of noise models to simulate the disturbances and defects of those images.

items.question: How do you assess the tradeoff of adding perception to a robot locomotion policy trained in simulation?
items.object: Perception in robot locomotion and the sim-to-real gap
items.answer: In the end, the final behavior is better if you do everything right. But that's a big if. The typical thing we refer to as the so-called sim-to-real gap: if you're training things in simulation and deploy them in real life, it's not the same. Things that work really well in simulation might not work at all in real life. That sim-to-real gap is much larger once you have perception in the loop. Once you're simulating either depth images or RGB images, it's even worse. That makes the job of the researcher or the engineer harder. You need to cross that sim-to-real gap for both the physics of the robot and the perceptive inputs. You have to simulate the sensors carefully. But if you do it right, then the final behavior is actually much better because you can see that the robot is not simply reacting to whatever is happening under its feet, but actually planning accordingly in advance.

items.question: How do you think about whether vision-based robot locomotion is a solved problem?
items.object: The boundary between robot locomotion and navigation
items.answer: It's interesting. It really depends where you draw the line on locomotion. Once the robot can cross complicated terrain, the next step goes more into navigation, which means: where should it go? Should it climb that thing, or should it avoid it? For now, everything I've described so far was mostly using geometry, so there are no semantics. But now, if you imagine the robot meaning a point A and a point B, and it's going to take the straight line and plow through whatever is between here and there, as opposed to thinking about which way to go—

items.question: Why do you think a robot’s locomotion policy needs semantics when it operates in an office?
items.object: Semantics in a robot’s locomotion policy
items.answer: If I imagine the robot walking behind me in the office, I don't really want it to climb on every single desk. I want it to avoid some things but also walk on others, right? If there's stairs, I want it to take the stairs, but I don't want it to hit plants or whatever else, which means that suddenly you have to add semantics to the policy.

items.question: Why do you think separating locomotion from semantic planning is probably the better short-term approach for robots?
items.object: Separating robot locomotion from semantic planning
items.answer: Once again, if you go from simulation to reality, it makes the sim-to-real gap bigger because suddenly you have to simulate all these offices, all these different objects. Plus, you probably need to give it images, not just depth images. You need to give it RGB images, which means you need to simulate it in a photoreal way. The other option, which is probably the more correct one in the short term, is to split the problem. You train the robot to be very good at walking on anything, but you don't give it semantic information, and you train another thing on top, which will be the planner or a higher-level policy that steers it around.

items.question: How do you view the tradeoff between end-to-end learning and a modular approach to robotics?
items.object: End-to-end learning versus modular approaches in robotics
items.answer: It's interesting because my whole PhD was about going more and more end to end for locomotion specifically, and still I'm here arguing that we should not do everything end to end. I think at some point we'll get there, but in the short and medium term, the more pragmatic approach is to split the problem and use different techniques for different parts of the problem.

I think at some point we'll get there, but in the short and medium term, as you said, the more pragmatic approach is to split the problem and use different techniques for different parts of the problem.

items.question: How do you think a reinforcement-learning planner’s reward should be defined for a robot operating around humans?
items.object: Reward functions for reinforcement-learning robot planners
items.answer: There are different ways to do this. If we still choose the RL route, we can train these planners with reinforcement learning, and typically we have to define this reward function. It would include things like don't hit anything, so avoid objects, and don't move too fast, because that's one thing that makes robots seem very dangerous. These reinforcement learning policies will try to optimize everything, so they will go very quickly to the goal. This is not really what we want with a robot that operates around humans. Typically we're actually trying to slow them down as much as possible. And that's mostly it. Then it depends on what is in front of the robot. There might be things that it's okay to walk on and others that it's not.

items.question: How do you see splitting robot locomotion from planning opening up other ways to train the planner?
items.object: Training a robot planner through imitation learning from human walking trajectories
items.answer: There is also another approach. Once you split the problem in half, you could train the locomotion with pure reinforcement learning in simulation, but train the planner with other data. For example, videos of humans walking around the office, and you can extract the trajectories from that. Then you don't really need reinforcement learning anymore. You train a behavior-cloning, imitation-learning policy that will just steer the robot like a human would walk.
quotes: There is also another approach. Once you split the problem in half, you could train the locomotion with pure reinforcement learning in simulation, but train the planner with other data. You train a behavior-cloning, imitation-learning policy that will just steer the robot like a human would walk.

The response proposes behavior cloning as a replacement for reinforcement learning when training the robot’s planner.

items.question: How do you see the transferability of reinforcement-learning techniques from quadruped to humanoid robots?
items.object: Transfer of reinforcement-learning techniques from quadruped to humanoid robots
items.answer: All of it transfers. That is the magic of reinforcement learning: these policies don't really care if they're controlling a quadruped or a humanoid. This was the big switch from a PhD to Flexion, where we're working mostly on humanoids. We've seen that the exact same techniques transfer.

items.question: What do you mean when you say locomotion learning transfers from quadrupeds to humanoid robots?
items.object: Transfer of locomotion learning techniques between robot forms
items.answer: When I say it transfers, the general techniques transfer; the models themselves don't. You for sure need to retrain a new policy, a new controller for the new robot. But if all your simulation pipelines are general enough, it can be as easy as changing the input file, the URDF that describes the robot, retraining it, then you're ready to deploy.

items.question: Why do you think tuning locomotion is harder for humanoid robots than for quadrupeds?
items.object: Human expectations of humanoid locomotion
items.answer: The tuning part is interesting because it is a little bit harder for humanoids compared to quadrupeds. I don't think it's really related to the fact that it has two or four legs or anything like that. Personally, I think it's mostly related to the fact that we have very specific expectations of how a humanoid robot should walk. Whereas a quadruped will, if it walks slightly differently from a dog, that's completely fine. But a humanoid, if it doesn't move the arms in the right way, if it bends the knees too much or walks a little bit sideways, humans have a very strong reaction to that.

items.question: How do you feel about the pace of progress across the robotics ecosystem?
items.object: The rapid progress of the robotics ecosystem
items.answer: First I want to say that it's really exciting that the whole ecosystem is moving so quickly. It feels like every single day there is a new video of a new robot doing something, and that's really good. We see a lot of progress both in hardware and on the AI side as well.

items.question: How do you assess what a video demonstration of a robot actually reveals about its capabilities?
items.object: Robot demonstrations and the capabilities they imply
items.answer: Typically, when I personally see a demo of a robot doing something, my approach is to think about what is the absolute easiest way to achieve that. That is typically how it's done. As an ecosystem, we're showing a vision of what robots should be doing, but behind the scenes it's sometimes a little bit different. For example, if you have a robot standing and doing some sort of manipulation on a table, folding sheets or something like that, typically one of two things is true. Either there is someone hiding behind the robot, behind a curtain somewhere in another room, teleoperating the robot, so it's not really autonomous. That's, let's say, one third of the cases. The other two thirds are where the robot is actually autonomous. But to get there, 100 people had to teleoperate 100 robots to collect a lot of data, hours and hours, in some cases thousands of hours, of robots doing very similar things in probably the same environment. They collect data, train a policy that can imitate that data, and then they're able to deploy robots autonomously, which is not exactly what you would see when you watch that video, because it feels like the robot can just adapt to anything and come to your home and do everything you're doing. We're just not there yet, but we'll get there soon.

items.question: Why do you see industrial use cases as a more practical focus for your robotics company than deployment in people's homes?
items.object: Industrial use cases for robots
items.answer: That's partially why, as a company, we're focusing more on industrial use cases. There are a lot of other challenges with industrial use cases because now performance is really important. You need to be very fast. You cannot slow everything down, at least in most cases. But you have a little bit more control over what's happening. For example, if we want to deploy 10 robots in a new warehouse, it's easier for us to send an engineer for one or two days to check that everything is in order, that they operate as they should. If they don't, fine-tune a few things and then let robots work, which is not something you can do in everyone's home.

items.question: What do you find interesting about the shift in how robot learning systems are trained on teleoperation data?
items.object: Pretrained vision and language encoders for learning robot actions from teleoperation data
items.answer: Typically it's supervised. You record the data: images of the camera and the commands that the teleoperator sent to the robot, which typically is how you should move your hands in space and how you should move your fingers. That is recorded, and then a big transformer is trained to produce the same actions from the same images. What I find interesting is the whole field shifted a little bit from just training these transformers from scratch to using vision and language encoders that were pretrained on internet-scale data.

items.question: How do you assess the value of pretrained language and vision encoders for helping robot policies generalize?
items.object: Pretrained language and vision encoders for robot policy generalization
items.answer: The general thought is that it helps with generalization, since the language and vision encoders were trained on internet-scale data and are supposed to generalize. A typical case was that if you don't do that, you would train a robot during the day, then if the lights go down at night, it won't be able to perform anymore. Even though there's still light and everything should just work—a human wouldn't even see the difference—but because the image embedding changes a bit, the policy doesn't perform anymore. I believe this gets better with the pretrained encoders. To be completely honest, the generalization capabilities overall still need to be proven.

items.question: What do you think it takes to successfully transfer a robot policy from simulation to the real world?
items.object: Crossing the sim-to-real gap in robotics
items.answer: You need to do a lot of things very explicitly. The challenge is that to cross the sim-to-real gap, you need to have a very deep understanding of both worlds: the simulation and how it works, and the real world. If I want to have a robot that walks around as it should in sim, I need to go very deep. I need to know exactly what's happening between a command that the policy outputs and all the way down to torque in the motors. There are typically 10 different layers of transformations, even just on software, of how we go from a high-level command to actual current in the motors. It's very tempting to ignore that. But by understanding every single layer and knowing all the different transformations, then you can properly simulate it. This really unlocks better performance.

items.question: How do you decide which physical details to include in a simulation for training a robot to operate in the real world?
items.object: The level of physical detail needed in robot simulation
items.answer: We have a very generic simulation environment, but there are some very specific things that are important. One clear example is the torque and velocity limits of a motor. You cannot expect it to do something that is not possible on the real robot, so you need to add those limits. There are a few more things like that, such as what kind of delay you can expect between a command. We are usually doing it in what we call a real-to-sim process. We take the real robot, hang it in the air, let it shake a little bit, collect data on all the different motors, and then we know which are those important effects that we need to identify. We identify them and add them to the simulator. But simulation speed is the most important thing, so you cannot afford to simulate all those different effects, currents, magnetic fields, etc. You need to abstract all of it away.

items.question: What have you learned about how difficult it is to switch to a new robot and make it walk?

items.answer: This was also the surprising part, one of the key learnings of this year: switching robots is fairly easy, as long as the hardware performs reasonably well. items.question: How do you see vision-language models helping robots handle the enormous variety of cooking tasks?
items.object: Using vision-language models to orchestrate robot task primitives
items.answer: You would never finish that, right? The set of tasks is huge. But what you could do is give the recipe to a VLM. You also give it images of what the robot sees. If the recipe says cut a cucumber, the VLM would say, “Grab the knife, grab the cucumber, and do this sort of motion to cut it.” Then you can break it down into much simpler primitives, like cutting things, holding a pan, putting it down somewhere, filling a glass of water, pouring it, things like that. Suddenly the set of these primitives is not infinite anymore. The challenge is that now we need a higher-level intelligence that will orchestrate all these primitives. items.question: How do you understand the relationship between a VLM’s reasoning capabilities and its ability to orchestrate a robot’s skills?
items.object: Using an off-the-shelf VLM to orchestrate robot skills
items.answer: It's similar. Maybe one way to describe this is, on our website we have two videos. We have a video of a robot walking in a forest and picking up trash. This is mostly there to showcase what's possible and also play a little bit on our Swiss angle, using our nature. We have another video where the robot is doing the same thing in our office. In that second video, it's 100% autonomous. You give it a text prompt. I think we're saying something like, “Pick up the toys in front of you and drop them in the basket at the end.” We're using an off-the-shelf VLM for that. The way this works is we're giving the images to the VLM and allowing it to call specific skills of the robot. The VLM would say, “Oh, I see a toy there on the ground. Let's walk to the toy.” “Let's walk to the toy” is a skill that is actually triggered and executed by the robot. Once we're there, it will trigger “pick up the toy,” then go to the basket and drop it off. By having a few of those primitives—which are walk to things, pick things up from the ground, and drop them somewhere else—we can recombine this in many different ways without any retraining, just by prompting an off-the-shelf VLM.

items.question: How do you envision a hierarchy of models turning an abstract robot task into motor control?
items.object: A hierarchical robot-control pipeline
items.answer: In our plan, if we go through that whole process, we train, let's say, 50 of those primitives. We distill everything. We are still developing a hierarchical pipeline where we have three models interacting with each other. It would start with a relatively large VLM that would not be allowed to use perception. The output of that one would be that the VLM would go from a very abstract task to clear subtasks, such that if you have a robot here and I tell it, “Go pick something up in the fridge,” it would say, “Turn around, go through the door, open the fridge, grab the thing, close the fridge,” etc. Clear instructions. Then those clear instructions would go to that VLA that we were describing before, where if it receives the instruction “open the fridge,” it will plan a kinematic motion for the arm to grab the fridge handle and open it just a few seconds into the future. Finally, we have what we call a whole-body tracker, which will receive this plan of how the hand should move and how the whole body should move, and then control the motors of that specific robot to execute that motion.

items.question: How do you understand the work involved in building a simulation environment for robot reinforcement learning beyond the simulator itself?
items.object: Simulator components and simulation training environments for robot reinforcement learning
items.answer: I guess you would add the RL algorithm as a third component that interacts with both, but that's it. The simulator itself is basically a physics engine and a renderer, and then you have to put a robot in there. If you wanted to walk on stairs, you have to create stairs, but you cannot just ask your robot to randomly figure out how to walk on very complex stairs. You have to create a whole curriculum of difficulty. You would start with very small stairs and progressively make them harder. The same is true for all sorts of tasks. When we're training a robot to open a door, we have to create a simulated version of the door, then help the robots. We have to figure out exactly all these training processes on top of just a scenario itself.

items.question: How do you see the role of value functions in robotics reinforcement learning today?
items.object: Value functions in robotics reinforcement learning
items.answer: Value functions are part of the RL algorithm itself. We're training, for example, mostly using some variant of PPO, which is an actor-critic algorithm. That means you're training both an actor and a critic. The critic is basically a value function. It's not used at deployment; it's only used to help the training of the actor during the training process. Now we're seeing some research into how it could actually be used even at deployment. I think this is more on the research side. It's not proven yet.

items.question: How do you judge the manual reward tuning involved in teaching robots to walk?
items.object: Task-derived reward tuning for robot locomotion
items.answer: About reward tuning, it is a big topic. We have 35 people in the company, and quite a few of these people still spend hours tuning rewards. Typically this is referred to in a negative way. You don't want people tuning rewards. But I think you have to make a distinction between two types of tuning. There are general rewards that simply come from the task itself. If we think again about how robots are walking, you would say the task is just go from point A to point B. But in reality it's a bit more complicated. You want the robot to go from point A to point B. You don't want it to use too much energy, hit the ground too hard, slip everywhere, or have the arms doing completely crazy motions around it. By the time you describe in text what you actually want, you already have maybe 15 lines. That translates to 15 different reward functions that you have to come up with and tune. My personal take is that part of tuning is fine.

items.question: Why do you try to avoid exploration-related reward tuning in robot reinforcement learning?
items.object: Exploration-related reward tuning in robot reinforcement learning
items.answer: There is another kind of tuning that tends to happen a lot in RL, related to exploration. Once you've described the perfect task you want, how do you guide the policy and the training process toward that? For example, if you want a robot that opens a door, you might need to tell it: put your hand close to the handle, close your fingers, then pull on the door. These are really things that don't scale across tasks. This is something we're trying to avoid as much as possible. That's why we're working on other techniques where we can use one or two demonstrations from a human to help the learning process instead of all these manually tuned reward functions.

items.question: How do you expect the deployment of humanoid robots doing useful work to unfold over the next several years?
items.object: The timeline and scaling of useful humanoid robot deployment
items.answer: I said before that I think there isn't a single humanoid robot providing value in the world today. My prediction is that will change around the end of next year, maybe beginning of 2027. It's hard to predict exactly what's going to happen, but I don't think we'll get this ChatGPT moment where suddenly you have a billion robots everywhere, just because you need to build the hardware. It doesn't scale like getting access to ChatGPT, right? I would predict that around the end of next year, we'll start seeing robots doing actual work. It will be just a few here and there, and then in 2027 and 2028, we'll scale both the numbers of robots per task and the set of different tasks that these robots can do. In the coming years we will go from hundreds of robots to thousands and then very quickly to millions, tens of millions, etc. And presumably you see that happening first in industrial settings and then consumer.

items.question: How do you think about the need for highly dexterous hands in humanoid robots?
items.object: Highly dexterous hands for humanoid robots
items.answer: One part where hardware is not there yet today is on the end effectors, on the hands. It's still debatable if you actually need very dexterous hands. I think one of the big reasons why many companies develop hands with high dexterity, like more than 20 degrees of freedom in a hand, is because they're using imitation learning. They're imitating humans, which means that you need to be able to imitate everything a human does. Once you go the other route, you can learn other kinds of behaviors with much simpler grippers. But the debate is still open on that.

items.question: How do you think about the right physical form for a robot intended to have human capabilities?
items.object: Robot form factors for achieving human capabilities
items.answer: I've worked on more than 25 robots by now, with any number of legs and arms imaginable, from zero to probably four, five, six legs, and there is room for all sorts of robots in the world. Honestly, I mostly use—and as a company we use—the word humanoid for lack of a better word. What we mean by that is not the human form factor but human capabilities. Very basically, we want robots that can go where humans go and can manipulate the environments in a similar way to how humans do that. You would probably need at least two arms with some sort of end effector to interact with the environment. Whether you have legs or wheels, both are fine. Both have their own applications. You can go a long way, especially in the industry, with a wheel platform. We're working with robots like that as well. Having said that, it's surprising how quickly wheeled platforms get stuck. A very common thing that's easy to imagine is if the floor is not perfectly flat, if you have cables or stairs, your wheel platform is stuck. Another very important part is the footprint. With those wheel platforms, you have two choices: either you make them very large, and then they're stable by default because they have a very large footprint, but they don't fit through tight spaces anymore. Very quickly, especially in slightly older industrial settings, you have tight spaces.

items.question: What do you see as the constraint on torso movement for robots with a small platform?
items.object: Small robot platforms and torso stability
items.answer: Typically what we see is that you just have a small platform, which means that you have to be very careful how you move the torso on top, because if you lean too far it just falls over.

items.question: What would you recommend as a starting robot for someone who wants to learn locomotion reinforcement learning?
items.object: Accessible robots for learning locomotion reinforcement learning
items.answer: For the locomotion reinforcement learning aspect, it's a little bit harder because you probably want a robot with legs, which also means the robots should be able to fall and stand up without completely breaking. I think the best bet there is the Chinese quadrupeds that are getting fairly cheap. It's still multiple thousands of dollars, but let's say it's affordable for a university or a school, or if you really want to go much deeper into that at home as well.

items.question: How would you approach experimenting with a quadruped robot after unboxing it?
items.object: Getting started with quadruped robot experiments
items.answer: When you unbox it, it can typically already do quite a lot. It will be able to walk. In some cases they even have things like a SLAM pipeline, so it can do some navigation, avoid obstacles, things like that. But then the challenge is that you want to get rid of all that software and basically recreate it from scratch. There again, there are many communities online and many GitHub repos that help you get started. The unitree is probably the most standard platform, so I would start there. There are people who open-source everything from training to deploying code, deploying these policies on those robots.
